undecided_findings.scenario: You open the player in Berlin. The privacy question waits at the bottom of the screen, over the lower part of the score. You drag your song 'Punk.gp' from the desktop towards the score. As you pass over the question box, 'Drop to open' disappears. You let go there anyway. undecided_findings.whats_wrong: The popup is rendered by web/app/layout.tsx, so it is not inside the player's drop zone. The drop zone accepts a drop only on itself and on the elements inside it, and nothing else on the page accepts one. A file dropped on the card therefore never reaches the player, and the browser handles the file itself (it opens or downloads it). Section 3 promises 'The player works while the card waits', and no case in section 9 drops a file on the card. The existing drop test runs in Sydney, where the card never shows.

undecided_findings.central_claim_check: Read web/app/play/PlayerShell.tsx. The drop handlers sit on the drop-zone <section> only: onDragEnter (:1046), onDragLeave (:1051), onDragOver (:1055) and onDrop (:1064). The only window-level listeners are dragend and pointermove (:957-967), and they only end the 'dragging' state; nothing cancels dragover or drop at window or document level. A search of web/app, web/lib and client/src finds no other dragover or drop handler. web/app/layout.tsx:15-27 renders the page and then the Toaster inside <body>, so a card rendered there is a sibling of the player's <main>, outside the drop zone. The comment beside the drop overlay (PlayerShell.tsx:1109-1113) records the same trap: an overlay mounted outside the container broke the drag counter, because 'every dragleave's relatedTarget was the overlay, which is not a descendant'. MDN's File drag and drop guide (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/HTML_Drag_and_Drop_API/File_drag_and_drop) says the browser may open or download a dropped file that no drop target accepts. Chromium change 8bee828 (https://crrev.com/8bee82851b8e9bc7ab7f049194ad259743db2c97), shipped in Chrome 85, makes such a drop open in a new tab instead of replacing the page. The existing drop test (web/e2e/player.e2e.ts:348) will run in Sydney once the config sets that time zone (section 1), so it never meets the card.
undecided_findings.contradicts: none — checked section 3 (Where, Non-blocking, Answering), section 1 (layout.tsx renders the card), section 9 (the No overlap case) and G7. pointer-events: none during a file drag changes nothing for clicks or the keyboard, and the card stays visible.

raw_constituents.title: The card over the drop zone swallows dropped files
raw_constituents.why_it_matters: A visitor in Europe who drops a score onto the part of the notation area under the card does not get it opened. The browser's default action runs instead: it opens or downloads the file, and a plain .xml score replaces the player in the tab. A comment beside the drop overlay in PlayerShell.tsx already records this problem: an element mounted outside the container is not a descendant, so dragleave throws off the player's drag counter and 'Drop to open' disappears over it. Add a Berlin case to privacy-choice.e2e.ts that drops a fixture onto the card's area while the card is showing and expects the file to open.

undecided_findings.title: Screen readers will not announce the popup when it appears
undecided_findings.severity_plain: should fix — a real gap an implementer will hit
undecided_findings.severity_note: Nothing crashes, but the spec's own promise ('announced politely') would be false in the obvious build, and only people who use screen readers pay for it.
undecided_findings.confidence_plain: double-checked by reading the spec, the repo and the sources; will be hit in practice (not all of it run)
undecided_findings.correction: One reason was overstated. An element can be a labelled region and also carry aria-live; nothing forbids both. The real problem is timing: the card arrives together with its text, and MDN's live-region guide says screen readers generally announce only changes to a live region that already exists (and that this varies between browsers and screen readers). So if the card itself is the live region, 'announced politely when it appears' will usually not happen. The fix is unchanged.

undecided_findings.scenario: You use a screen reader and open Notation Hero in Berlin. A moment after the page loads, a privacy question appears at the bottom of the screen. Your screen reader says nothing about it. Unless you happen to find it, you never learn that the site is asking for your consent, and the question comes back on every visit.
undecided_findings.whats_wrong: Section 3 says the card is 'announced politely when it appears'. The obvious way to build that is aria-live on the card itself. But the card is added to the page together with its text, after hydration, and a live region that arrives with its text is generally not announced. The repo met this before in PlayerShell.tsx and solved it with an empty live region that stays on the page. Neither the unit tests nor the axe scan in section 9 would notice the silence.

When the card appears, its question arrives as a change to a live region that already exists, which is the case screen readers announce. It is the pattern PlayerShell.tsx already uses for 'Opened …' and for a failed open, so there is nothing new to invent.

plain_terms.live region: a part of the page that a screen reader reads out when its text changes, without the person moving to it
plain_terms.polite: the screen reader waits for a pause instead of interrupting
plain_terms.hydration: the moment the page's code starts running in the browser, after the first HTML has arrived
plain_terms.labelled region: a named area of the page ('Privacy choice') that screen-reader users can jump to
plain_terms.axe: the automated accessibility checker used in the web job
plain_terms.role=\"alert\": a live region for urgent messages, read out at once, interrupting the screen reader

undecided_findings.central_claim_check: web/app/play/PlayerShell.tsx:1235-1242 keeps an always-mounted, visually hidden paragraph with aria-live="polite". Its comment says: 'a live region added to the DOM at the same moment its text appears is not announced at all — the region has to be there first.' MDN's ARIA live regions guide (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/Accessibility/ARIA/Guides/Live_regions) gives the same advice: create the region empty first, change its text later, and put it in the page's first HTML for the most reliable result. The card can only appear after hydration (spec line 445), because the time zone and the saved answer are known only in the browser. MDN notes one exception: role="alert" is usually announced even when it is inserted with its text, but it interrupts the screen reader, is often read with the word 'Alert' first, and is meant for urgent messages, so it does not fit a polite question.
undecided_findings.contradicts: none — checked section 3 (Screen readers, Non-blocking), section 9 (the PrivacyChoices unit tests and the axe scan with the popup open), 'To verify at plan time' (no layout shift: a visually hidden region takes no space) and section 2's rule that nothing shows when neither key is set (an empty, silent region shows nothing).

spike.why: Whether speech happens needs a real screen reader (VoiceOver or NVDA) and a person listening; a headless browser cannot tell. The behaviour is stated by the repo's own comment and by MDN. raw_constituents.title: Screen-reader announcement of the card will not happen
raw_constituents.why_it_matters: European screen-reader users may never be told that a privacy question has appeared: the card is inserted after hydration, and a live region that arrives together with its text is not announced. `web/app/play/PlayerShell.tsx` records exactly this ("the region has to be there first") and keeps an always-mounted `aria-live` paragraph for it. A labelled region is a landmark, not a live region, so one element cannot be both "a labelled region" and "announced politely when it appears", and neither the unit tests nor the axe scan the spec lists would notice the silence. The repo's own pattern, a persistent polite region that receives text when the card mounts, closes the gap.
raw_constituents.suggested_fix: In section 3, replace the Screen readers bullet with: 'The card is a labelled region ("Privacy choice") and carries no `aria-live` of its own. `PrivacyChoices` renders an empty polite live region from the first render and keeps it for the life of the page, the way `PlayerShell.tsx` keeps its `announcement` paragraph; when the card appears, the region receives the question text.' Add to the `PrivacyChoices` unit tests that the live region is in the document before the card appears and that its text changes when the card appears.

undecided_findings.central_claim_check: Read the 2026-10-05 spike (throwaway, not in the repo). Its instrumentation-client.ts queued gtag('consent', 'default', {…}) and then gtag('set', { allow_google_signals: false, allow_ad_personalization_signals: false }): a separate settings step. Its js and config calls came from @next/third-parties 16.3.6's GoogleAnalytics component, whose inline script calls gtag('js', new Date()) and then gtag('config', <ID>) with no settings object (checked in the published package, https://unpkg.com/@next/third-parties@16.3.6/dist/google/ga.js). So the queue the spike ran was consent, set, js, then config with only the ID. The spec's sketch (lines 182-193) has no set step and puts the two settings inside config, a shape the spike never ran. Google's privacy-controls guide (https://developers.google.com/tag-platform/security/guides/privacy) documents both places for these two settings (set for every tag on the page, config for one property), so the sketch is not wrong, only unverified while the spec calls it verified.

fyi_observations.correction: The effect holds; the reason given is out of date. WebKit's 2019 rule capped cookies written by a script at a 7-day expiry (Intelligent Tracking Prevention, ITP 2.1). A 2022 WebKit release removed that cap and now deletes cookies written by a script, together with all other storage a script can write (localStorage too), when the site gets no click, tap or key press during 7 days of browser use. So a visitor who returns after a week without using the site still counts as new, and the same rule also deletes the saved privacy answer, so a visitor in Europe is asked again.
